text:
The true story of the fall of the Aztec empire

The few hundred Spaniards did not overthrow the Mexica empire by themselves. The Mexica, later called Aztecs, did not throw down their weapons because they took Cortés for a god.

In 1519 the Mexica sat at the center of a tributary empire in the Basin of Mexico. Their capital was Tenochtitlan, a lake city of causeways, canoes, temples, and markets. Together with Texcoco and Tlacopan they formed the Triple Alliance. Subject towns sent maize, cotton, labor, and captives. That world was old, crowded, and already full of enemies.

The first Spaniards did not walk into that capital. They reached the Maya coast years earlier. What follows is the campaign in chronological order, not the popular narrative of an unaided European miracle.

The story begins before Cortés. In 1511 a Spanish ship out of Darién wrecked in the Caribbean. Survivors drifted to the Yucatán shore and fell into Maya hands. Most died. Two did not. Gonzalo Guerrero married into a Maya community, had children, took on Maya life, and later refused to rejoin Spaniards. Gerónimo de Aguilar, a man in religious orders, lived about eight years as a captive and then as a go-between. He learned Yucatec Maya well enough to live in it. When people say he became basically Maya, they mean language, dress, endurance, and years inside a Maya town, not that he ceased to be a Spaniard in law or faith. Maya Yucatán was not the Mexica empire. Maya languages are not Nahuatl. There was no single Maya emperor in a lake capital. That distinction matters, because the road to Tenochtitlan began here.

Across the water, Cuba was already a Spanish base and already a disappointment. Gold on the island was thin. Settlers wanted richer land to the west. The governor was Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar. He meant for the next discoveries to remain his enterprise. The credit at court was to be his, the share of treasure was to be his to distribute, and the commander in the field was not to eclipse him. Cortés later became the rival he most feared, the subordinate who would take the fame Velázquez wanted for himself.

In 1517 Velázquez permitted a private venture to sail under Francisco Hernández de Córdoba, about 110 men who paid for their own ships. One of them was Bernal Díaz del Castillo, a Castilian infantryman from Medina del Campo who had come to the islands in search of advancement. He is the reason the Spanish rank-and-file side of this story can still be followed in detail. He was not a court historian and not a priest. He sailed on this voyage, on Grijalva’s voyage the next year, and then with Cortés. Late in life, as a minor encomendero in Guatemala, he composed The True History of the Conquest of New Spain to answer Francisco López de Gómara and the letters of Cortés, which presented the captain as a solitary genius. Díaz records horses, wounds, hunger, disputes, and temples. He is also late, partial, and proud. He is most useful as a witness from the column, not as an impartial record of the war.

Before Córdoba’s men sailed they took a priest, heard Mass, and commended themselves to God and the Virgin. That choice was not ornamental. A company far from a parish wanted confession, the sacrament, and burial rites if the voyage failed. A priest also conferred a claim to lawfulness. Spanish theory held that pagans should be summoned to peace, the crown, and baptism before war could be called just. According to Díaz, Velázquez asked them to raid the Guanajes Islands for slaves. Díaz says the crew refused, answering that neither God nor the king had commanded them to turn free people into slaves. The priest made that refusal easier to defend.

They made landfall in the Maya world. They saw stone towns larger than anything in the islands, walked into temple courts with blood on the altars, and were ambushed by organized fighters. At Champotón they were nearly destroyed. Córdoba later died of his wounds. The survivors returned to Cuba impoverished and badly cut up, carrying the only news that mattered. There were kingdoms to the west.

In 1518 Juan de Grijalva tested that report, again along Maya shores. Díaz sailed with him. Traces of gold, large towns, and determined resistance all pointed the same way. Velázquez began fitting a larger expedition and first named Hernán Cortés to command it. Cortés was his secretary, a man of the Cuban colony, able to raise ships and investors quickly. Then Velázquez reconsidered. Cortés was gathering too many men, spending too freely, and speaking like a commander who meant to keep both the land and the credit. 

The governor moved to revoke the commission rather than let his own captain become the hero of the discovery. Cortés did not wait to be detained. In February 1519 he sailed in haste, still displaying Velázquez’s authority on paper and already planning to sever that dependence.

That first Cortés company was small: on the order of 500 soldiers, about 100 sailors, a dozen or so horses, a few light cannon, and a modest number of harquebuses. A harquebus, sometimes spelled arquebus, was an early matchlock firearm. It was long, heavy, and slow to serve. A smoldering cord lit the powder. A man might fire once, then spend a long minute reloading. The guns were inaccurate beyond close range, useless in hard rain, and few on this march. They produced noise and smoke and could pierce cotton armor at short distance. They were not later infantry firearms. Crossbows were often more reliable. Swords, lances, and horses accounted for more of the daily killing.

The small band myth takes those 1519 figures and treats them as the entire war. It holds that this modest European force, acting with little help, overthrew the Mexica empire. The landing roster was real. The unaided triumph was not. The rest of the timeline shows why.

Along the Maya coast Cortés recovered Aguilar near Cozumel. Aguilar could speak Maya and Spanish, not Nahuatl. At Tabasco, among Chontal Maya towns, the Spaniards won a hard fight at Centla. Local lords gave food, cloth, and twenty women. One was Malinalli, baptized Marina and remembered as Malinche. She was Nahua by birth, had been moved into the Maya zone, and spoke Nahuatl and Maya. For a time the chain ran from Cortés to Aguilar in Spanish, from Aguilar to Marina in Maya, and from Marina to Mexica envoys in Nahuatl. Then she acquired Spanish and the middle step fell away. Without this Maya chapter there is no Aguilar, and without Aguilar and Marina there is no rapid diplomacy with the Mexica. Yucatán itself would require decades of later campaigns. Its part here is first contact, first bloodshed, and the linguistic bridge inland.

On the Mexican shore Cortés founded Villa Rica de la Vera Cruz and had the new town council name him captain general in the name of Charles V. A municipality answerable to the king need not obey a governor in Cuba. He sent letters and a share of treasure directly to Spain so that the emperor would hear Cortés’s name, not Velázquez’s, as the author of the enterprise. He scuttled or disabled the ships so his men could not slip back to Velázquez. The story that he burned them is too tidy. The purpose was the same. There would be no quiet return to Santiago de Cuba.

The Totonacs of Cempoala listened because they lived under Mexica exactions. Cortés offered gifts, threats, Mass, and a new alignment. Marina made negotiation possible once speech shifted from Maya to Nahuatl. She was coerced. She was also the political hinge of the war.

Tlaxcala came next. It was a league of altepetl that had resisted the Triple Alliance for generations, and it is here that the small band myth first fails against the evidence. Cortés did not receive an alliance on the first day. The Tlaxcalans met him with large armies. Cavalry, steel, and the report of those few matchlocks shocked them. They did not kneel because a horse looked supernatural or because a gun made thunder. They tested the newcomers, then their leaders made a calculated choice. They would use the strangers against an old enemy. From that hour every Spanish march depended on Indigenous food, porters, scouts, and warriors. A few hundred Castilians could not provision themselves across the highlands or replace their dead. 
Tlaxcala supplied that capacity.
At Cholula, a major religious city tied to the Mexica world, Cortés said he had uncovered a plot and oversaw a massacre in the temple precinct. Spanish accounts call it preemption. Indigenous memory calls it slaughter. Both descriptions can stand. Nearby cities learned the terms of the new coalition.

In November 1519 the company walked the causeway into Tenochtitlan. Cortés did not enter with Spaniards alone. He entered with a Spanish core and a much larger Tlaxcalan escort. The lake city astonished Díaz and the rest: canoes, palaces, the Templo Mayor, a market that seemed to hold a kingdom’s worth of goods.  Later books favor enormous population figures. Some sixteenth-century observers spoke more modestly of tens of thousands. The city was vast, dense, rich, and vulnerable because it stood on water and lived from tribute.

The Mexica did not govern a modern nation-state. Subject cities kept their own lords and grudges. Tribute and captives held the system together. Flower wars and battlefield captures fed a sacred and political machine. Human sacrifice was real. Mexica books, temple archaeology, and Spanish testimony all document it. Spanish body counts were often inflated. The rite was not a colonial invention. That machine is why so many towns were prepared to help dismantle Tenochtitlan.

Moteuczoma Xocoyotzin received the strangers. Cortés later needed a defensible account for the king after defying Velázquez, so the letters have the emperor submit and assign the moral work to prophecy. The claim that Moteuczoma yielded because he took Cortés for Quetzalcoatl is a weak explanation of 1519 statecraft. So is the story that Mexica warriors saw pale men and laid down their arms. Hospitality is not worship. Receiving ambassadors is not abdication. 

Moteuczoma housed them, observed them, and tried to manage armed foreigners together with subject cities already beginning to detach. If the city had believed it was entertaining gods, what followed would be unintelligible.

Months of strained coexistence followed. Velázquez then spent a fortune trying to recover both the land and the credit. The decisive instrument was Pánfilo de Narváez, sent in 1520 with a force often put at about 900 to 1,400 men and some nineteen ships, with orders to seize Cortés. 

Narváez landed near Veracruz. Cortés left a garrison in Tenochtitlan under Pedro de Alvarado and marched to the coast. In a night rain at Cempoala he captured Narváez, who lost an eye. Most of Narváez’s men changed sides. Velázquez had meant to destroy the man who was stealing his reputation. He instead furnished the additional Spaniards that the small band myth omits. He also introduced a catastrophe he did not intend. Smallpox arrived with that fleet, likely through an enslaved African man in Narváez’s company.

While Cortés was absent, Alvarado’s garrison slaughtered participants at the Toxcatl ceremony. The city rose. Moteuczoma died in the rupture. Spaniards said his own people struck him. Mexica tradition said the Spaniards killed him. The question remains open. The coalition then fled on the night called La Noche Triste. Men died on the causeways under stones and arrows. Some drowned with gold they would not abandon. Indigenous allies died beside them. This was not a handful of knights against a crowd that had forgotten how to fight. Matchlocks were of little use on a packed, wet causeway.

Cortés survived because Tlaxcala still wanted the war. He rebuilt with the very men Velázquez had sent to bind him. More ships arrived from the islands. By August 1521 there were, on a careful modern estimate, on the order of 900 Spaniards around the ruined capital. Across the whole war some 2,500 to 3,000 Spaniards had likely set foot in Mexico. Many died. Even those totals were a minority. The force that returned was a league of altepetl with a Spanish command group attached. Allied fighters in the final siege are best counted in the tens of thousands. Some estimates run much higher. When Texcoco changed sides, the coalition gained canoes, shipwrights, and a lake ally. That defection did more to isolate Tenochtitlan than any single Spanish volley.

Smallpox killed Cuitlahuac and emptied houses before the final siege. Disease did not decide the war by itself. Cortés had already fought inland and entered the capital before the epidemic reached its height there. Omit the epidemic and the campaign looks cleaner than it was.

In 1521 the siege was slow and savage. Indigenous labor built the brigantines that closed the lake. Allied warriors carried the landward fighting. Cannon on the ships mattered more than the old harquebuses had on the inland march. Causeways became killing grounds. Houses came down block by block. Famine finished the rest. Cuauhtemoc fought until his capture on 13 August 1521. The city on the water was a ruin. 

Survivors were branded, allotted, baptized, and taxed. Spanish captains took women, metal, and encomiendas. Allied cities took revenge and a new place in the colonial order. Tlaxcala extracted privileges it would defend for a long time. Far to the east, Maya towns that had first met Córdoba remained unconquered.

Velázquez continued to litigate. He wanted Cortés condemned as a rebel and Mexico returned to Cuban jurisdiction, so that the conquest would stand in the record as Velázquez’s work rather than Cortés’s. Cortés continued to send gold and letters to Charles V. The crown preferred a conquered province to a governor’s wounded pride. Velázquez never governed Mexico and never received the credit he had tried to reserve for himself. He died in Santiago de Cuba in 1524 still pursuing the case. Cortés received titles, then learned that kings distrust men who seize kingdoms without authorization.

Who, then, overthrew the Mexica empire? If the question asks who addressed the king and claimed the province, Cortés did, after appropriating Velázquez’s commission and then defeating the army sent to recover it. If the question asks whether a few hundred Spaniards accomplished the conquest unaided, the answer is no. The fighters who filled the streets were Tlaxcalans, Totonacs, Texcocans after their rupture with the Mexica, Huexotzincans, and other polities with old scores to settle. Steel, horses, a few firearms, and lake artillery intensified a war those cities were already prepared to wage. The Mexica did not surrender Tenochtitlan to visiting gods. They lost a coalition war after plague, famine, the defection of subject towns, and a siege that lasted months.

Two tired traditions still flatten the sequence. One casts every Spaniard as a unique monster and every Mesoamerican city as a garden. The other repeats the small band myth, adds the tale of divine mistaken identity, and treats Mexica sacrifice as the only cruelty worth naming. Both are inadequate. The Mexica conducted an expansionist sacrificial empire. The Spaniards conducted an expansionist Christian empire that enslaved and extracted, and they spent nearly as much energy fighting Velázquez as they spent fighting Tenochtitlan. Subject peoples chose the alliance they thought they could survive. Many misjudged how complete Spanish dominion would become. Their choice remained a choice, and their numbers remained the numbers that took the city.

text:
One man offered diplomacy without surrender. The other offered life or hell.

Daniel Davis put Patrick Henningsen of 21st Century Wire on the UN week and the two speeches that will not sit in the same sentence. Iranian President Pezeshkian told the General Assembly he is open to talks and will not surrender. Trump told the same building he can obliterate the country or grant it a future, that they refused his generosity, that Midnight Hammer buried the nuclear file under rubble, and that a deal waits until after the midterms because he is not running.

Henningsen’s read is that the threat did not scare Tehran. It handed Pezeshkian the rebuttal. State terror, in his framing, is the power that bombs, denies, funds proxies, then lectures the hall on terrorism. The sharper shock, he says, is the silence. G7 partners who live on UN-charter language. Democrats who would have called the same paragraph a war crime from the other party. Applause in the room for a binary of deal or annihilation.

Davis presses the history. Offered talks, they refused, we struck. Henningsen says there is no clean record of that clemency-for-program bargain, and the administration keeps the word nuclear deliberately fogged so a civilian program and a weapons dash can be treated as one. Worse, in Davis’s line: pretend to negotiate, bomb in the middle, twice. An MOU signed like theater and then broken. Washington then repeats that Iran cannot be trusted. The bases that answered are the ones that are gone.

Two theaters. NATO talk against Russia thick enough to smell. West Asia still on fire. A president who ran against forever wars now speaking as if a nation’s existence is a personal decision. That is not leverage. That is a world that will not bend to the speech.

Watch it. Surrender is not a diplomatic term. Annihilation is not a midterm calendar item.

🇺🇲 🇮🇷 @citrinowicz published this nine days before the war started, before a single strike had landed. Seven months later, after a war that began by doing exactly what he warned against most specifically, it reads less like analysis than a checklist Washington proceeded to run through.

Start with his sixth scenario: targeting Khamenei directly. Citrinowicz called it the most unpredictable option, one that could trigger uncontrolled retaliation and “just as easily radicalize” the regime as moderate it.

The war opened on February 28 with exactly that decapitation strike. It wasn't a later escalatory option debated mid-conflict. It was the opening move.

The rest of his framework has tracked the war with similar accuracy.

Regime change was never seriously attempted, and there was no viable opposition to install, exactly as he wrote. There has been no internal uprising. Levada polling we covered weeks ago instead showed a population that “withdrew into acceptance” rather than revolt, precisely the alternative to democratic transition that he had flagged.

The nuclear program wasn't eliminated; it was obscured. The IAEA's September report cannot verify Iran's uranium stockpile or locate a facility Iran announced more than a year ago. “Delayed, not permanently removed,” Citrinowicz wrote. Seven months later, that describes the IAEA's operational reality.

The missile program survived as well. Iran was still launching strikes this month and is separately building a new ramjet-propelled anti-ship missile with Russian help. Citrinowicz predicted that the program would be rebuilt “with greater determination.” He could not have specifically foreseen the outside assistance, but the underlying logic has held.

His warning about negotiations may be the most consequential. Military pressure, he wrote, could “harden Iran's negotiating position or eliminate diplomatic channels entirely” rather than produce concessions.

Seven months later, the June MOU collapsed within weeks. Ratcliffe's covert Moscow trip produced a trilateral summit proposal Iran has shown no real urgency to accept. And Iran's posture, according to the Kimmage and Lipman essay we covered last week, is built around Putin-style endurance rather than capitulation.

Tehran has followed the path Citrinowicz warned was possible.

What stands out about the piece is not one prediction landing. Citrinowicz offered a six-point, falsifiable framework before a shot was fired. Seven months of war have yet to produce a scenario in which the results exceeded what he argued military force could realistically achieve.

“Military capability is not the same as strategic advantage” was his thesis. Seven months later, it remains a useful lens through which to assess the war.

text:
Abscam (Arab scam) was a famous Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) undercover sting operation conducted between 1978 and 1980 that exposed widespread political corruption and bribery. In 1979, the operation shifted focus to public corruption, using hidden cameras and audio gear in hotels, yachts, and townhouses to offer cash bribes to public officials in exchange for political favors, gambling licenses, and immigration help... 

In 1978–1980, the FBI launched 'Abscam', an undercover sting designed to expose political corruption. Agents created a fake Middle Eastern company called “Abdul Enterprises”, fronted by a fictional Arab sheikh who supposedly wanted to invest millions in U.S. ventures. The FBI then approached politicians with offers of cash in exchange for political favors, immigration help, business approvals, and legislative influence.

What followed was astonishing: several members of Congress, including one senator and multiple representatives, accepted bribes on camera. Some stuffed cash into their pockets, some negotiated price points, and some openly promised to deliver political favors. In total, seven congressmen were convicted, along with local officials, making it one of the largest corruption scandals in U.S. political history.

The fallout was explosive. Supporters of the sting argued it exposed real corruption; critics claimed the FBI had crossed ethical lines by creating temptation rather than uncovering existing crimes. But the courts upheld the convictions, and Abscam became a defining moment in modern American political accountability, a rare instance where a quarter of the politicians tested were caught taking the bait.

Beyond the headline‑grabbing bribery tapes, Abscam also exposed how deeply informal networks shaped Washington. Several lawmakers weren’t caught because they were “clean,” but because they quietly warned colleagues to stay away from the mysterious sheikh , revealing an undercurrent of whispered caution that never made the news. The FBI later admitted that these off‑camera refusals, tip‑offs, and back‑channel conversations painted a far more complicated picture of Congress: not just who took the money, but who sensed something was rotten and steered clear.

text:
In the Marvel superhero universe Carnage is not just another symbiote villain or a red-colored version of Venom. He is the purest expression of chaotic evil the symbiote concept has ever produced, a walking engine of random murder and nihilistic freedom that terrifies even other monsters. While casual fans might know the name from movies or games as a loud, blade-swinging psycho in a living red suit, the full comic truth reveals something far deeper, more disturbing, and cosmically horrifying. Carnage is the result of a perfect, cellular-level merger between the worst human being imaginable and an alien offspring of the Venom symbiote, and over decades of stories that merger has pulled in ancient gods, cults, codices of living darkness, and even attempts at godhood itself.

The human half of this nightmare is Cletus Kasady, a man whose entire existence reads like a catalog of atrocity and philosophical emptiness. He was born inside the Ravencroft Institute for the criminally insane to a mother with severe paranoid schizophrenia. She died shortly after his birth under circumstances that remain murky even in the records, possibly tied to her trying to harm the infant or suffering violence around him. As a child he was placed with an abusive guardian, often described as his grandmother, whom he killed by pushing her down a flight of stairs. Later placements with his father Roscoe and mother or stepmother Louise ended in more horror. Cletus tortured and killed the family dog out of jealous rage, believing it received more affection than he did. This triggered a beating in which his father killed or nearly killed his mother, and young Cletus offered no defense or help during the subsequent trial, contributing to his father's execution.

Orphaned, Cletus was sent to the St. Estes Home for Boys. There he endured constant bullying from other children and brutal discipline from staff. He formed one fleeting friendship with a boy named Billy Bentine who took the blame for a fire Cletus had started as a prank, but overall the environment only sharpened his antisocial hatred. In his teenage years a girl he developed feelings for rejected him harshly. He responded by pushing her in front of an oncoming school bus. His ultimate act of revenge was setting the entire orphanage ablaze, murdering the disciplinarian administrator and many of the bullies who had tormented him. These events cemented his core belief system: life is meaningless and futile, laws and morality are nothing but empty words invented to cage people, and the only real freedom comes from embracing pure, random, unpatterned chaos through bloodshed. In his mind killing does not end lives, it liberates victims from the prison of ordered existence. He would later describe his murders as setting people free.

As an adult Cletus became a cannibalistic serial killer responsible for numerous unsolved murders in addition to the ones that finally caught up with him. He received eleven consecutive life sentences and was locked away at Ryker's Island. It was there, sharing a cell with Eddie Brock, that the next chapter began. Eddie at that point was separated from his own symbiote and dealing with his own fractured life. Cletus, ever sociable in his twisted way, tried to befriend Eddie and convert him to the same nihilistic gospel of chaos and meaninglessness. He spoke openly about how there is no good or evil, only power and the joy of doing whatever one wants. Eddie rejected the overtures violently and beat him. Cletus simply smiled through it, seeing even rejection as part of the meaningless game.

The transformation happened during a chaotic jailbreak triggered by the return of the Venom symbiote coming to reclaim Eddie. In the violence and confusion a small piece of symbiote biomass, an asexually spawned offspring, made contact with Cletus through a cut or wound. Instead of a surface-level bonding like most symbiote hosts experience, this new symbiote merged directly into Cletus's bloodstream and integrated with his biology on a cellular level. The change was almost instantaneous. Cletus Kasady became Carnage. He escaped the prison in a bloody frenzy, killing guards and beginning a killing spree that would define him as one of Spider-Man's most personal and terrifying foes. His first notable victim outside was a graduate student at Empire State University who happened to be friends with Peter Parker, immediately making the conflict intimate for Spider-Man.

What makes Carnage unique among symbiote hosts is the depth and seamlessness of this merger. Most symbiotes bond externally or with some resistance, creating the famous internal dialogue and power struggles seen with Venom and Eddie Brock. The Carnage symbiote did not just ride along or amplify traits. It became part of Cletus's blood and DNA from the very beginning. This allowed abilities that feel more innate and horrifying: Carnage can harden and project his own blood into blades, axes, spears, and tendrils that shoot from his body. He can create independent constructs, form shifting armor and monstrous shapes, and regenerate from catastrophic damage that would kill almost anything else. He survived being ripped in half by the Sentry and kept going. Because the bond is cellular he refers to himself in the singular "I" rather than the plural "we" that Venom uses. There is no meaningful separation or moral tug-of-war. Cletus's bottomless sadism, his complete lack of empathy or restraint, and his philosophical commitment to chaos found their perfect counterpart in a symbiote built for violence and corruption. The result is not a conflicted anti-hero or a tragic monster. It is a single entity that lives only to spread death and disorder, and it enjoys every second of it.

Early stories kept Carnage mostly street-level but already apocalyptic in tone. He clashed repeatedly with Spider-Man, who often needed help from Venom, the Fantastic Four, or other heroes to contain him because Carnage had no rules, no hesitation, and superior raw power in many direct confrontations. He was locked in high-security facilities like the Vault and Ravencroft only to escape again and again. One of the defining early sagas was the Maximum Carnage crossover. After another escape, aided by experiments on his blood, Carnage assembled a small army of fellow monsters and psychopaths. He partnered with Shriek, a woman gifted with devastating sonic screams and psychic influence who became his lover and ideological soulmate, sharing his love of driving people into murderous insanity. They recruited Doppelganger, a grotesque multi-armed spider-like duplicate; Demogoblin, a demonic goblin entity; and Carrion, a plague carrier. Using Shriek's powers to spread waves of fear and madness across New York, they turned the city into a war zone of riots, mass killings, and collapsing order. Heroes from multiple Spider-Man books, including Captain America and others, had to unite to stop the rampage. Carnage treated the entire event as performance art, the ultimate proof that chaos is the only honest state of the world.

Over the years Carnage has built a kind of grotesque family. Besides Shriek and Doppelganger he has spawned or influenced other symbiotes, most notably during a fight with Venom when his symbiote gave birth to a new one that bonded with police officer Patrick Mulligan and became Toxin. Carnage viewed this "offspring" with twisted paternal feelings mixed with the desire to destroy it before it could grow strong enough to challenge him, leading to uneasy temporary alliances with Venom. He has taken over entire towns, most memorably in the Carnage, U.S.A. story where he and his spawn infected the population of Doverton, Colorado, turning it into a controlled symbiote nightmare state until heroes intervened. He has assimilated other symbiotes, survived multiple "deaths," and continued killing even when temporarily separated from his symbiote by painting himself red and operating as a purely human monster.

The story deepens dramatically when the true origins of the symbiotes enter the picture. They are not simply alien parasites that arrived on Earth by chance. They were created by Knull, a primordial god of darkness and the living abyss who existed before the current universe. When the Celestials brought light and structured creation into the void, Knull saw it as an invasion of his domain. He forged the All-Black Necrosword from his own shadow and the severed head of a Celestial and waged war against life itself. To conquer and corrupt, he shaped the symbiotes from living darkness as weapons and extensions of his will. He built a hive mind on the artificial planet Klyntar and sent symbiote dragons and hordes across the cosmos. Some symbiotes eventually bonded with more noble hosts on Earth and rebelled, using their combined power to imprison Knull inside Klyntar itself, turning his former throneworld into his cage. The Venom symbiote and its lineage carry this ancient heritage but many broke free of Knull's direct influence and chose their own paths.

Knull is the mysterious, little-known character that only dedicated comic readers fully grasp in relation to Carnage. Until relatively recent events most fans knew symbiotes as cool but ultimately Earth-bound alien suits with weaknesses to sound and fire. The deeper truth is that every symbiote traces back to this arrogant, sadistic, primordial entity who wants to unmake all creation and return the universe to primordial void and darkness. He is the dark father behind the entire race, and Carnage, as one of the most violent and unrestrained offspring, became the perfect vector for his influence to return.

This connection exploded into the foreground during the Absolute Carnage event. After one of Cletus's many deaths a cult devoted to Knull, led by a corrupted Scorn, retrieved his body and a piece of the ancient Grendel symbiote, a dragon-like primordial symbiote tied directly to Knull from the earliest ages. They bonded it to Cletus, reanimating him as an undead being psychically linked to the dark god. Knull spoke to him, viewing the serial killer as a potential apostle or tool to accelerate his freedom. Cletus resisted full control. He consumed codices, the tiny remnants of living symbiote abyss left in the spines of anyone who has ever hosted a symbiote, living or dead. Each codex made him stronger and more connected to the hive. He reshaped the Grendel biomass into his classic Carnage appearance, gathered old allies including Shriek and Doppelganger, and set out to harvest more codices while building a following. He became Dark Carnage, a towering skeletal monstrosity marked with Knull's spiral, capable of city-threatening power. The plan nearly succeeded in fully awakening Knull, but Venom ultimately killed Dark Carnage. Ironically that death helped sever the final restraints and allowed Knull to break free completely, leading directly into the King in Black invasion where the dark god coated Earth in living abyss and nearly conquered the planet.

Even after these events Carnage has continued evolving in more recent stories. The symbiote entity has at times pursued its own path toward godhood, forming a Cult of Carnage composed of the depraved and murderous who worship the red chaos. It has sought or created clones of Cletus Kasady as hosts to ground its expanding perspective, because pure symbiote divinity apparently needs a human anchor to fully express its will in the physical world. Carnage has clashed with forces trying to contain symbiote threats, escalated vendettas against the Brock family and anti-symbiote agents, and positioned itself as an ascending dark power building its own congregation of killers.

Through all the resurrections, power escalations, and brushes with cosmic entities, Cletus Kasady's fundamental nature never changes. He remains the man who sees beauty only in slaughter, who believes random violence is the highest art form, and who treats every death as both liberation for the victim and proof of his own freedom. He has bonded with more symbiotes than almost any other character, survived being eaten, burned, ripped apart, and launched into space, and still returns grinning. The cellular bond that created him made the symbiote not a suit or a parasite but an extension of his own blood and will. That is why Carnage feels different from every other symbiote story. Venom can be a hero. Other hosts struggle and sometimes overcome. Carnage simply is. He is the logical endpoint of what happens when an entity designed for corruption and violence meets a human soul that was already there waiting for it with open arms and a philosophy that celebrates the void.

This is the full picture only hardcore readers piece together across decades of comics. The surface-level red killing machine is real, but underneath lies a man whose childhood forged a monster, a bonding that erased any separation between host and symbiote, a personal war on meaning itself, and a connection to an ancient darkness that nearly unmade reality. Carnage does not want to rule the world or conquer heroes for glory. He wants to prove, one random murder at a time, that nothing matters except the beautiful freedom of chaos. And in the Marvel universe that makes him one of the most uniquely terrifying forces in existence.

text:
Twenty-three governments. One year. One database tracking all of them doing more or less the same thing: reaching across borders to silence people who had the nerve to leave.

Freedom House's transnational repression records for 2013 are worth sitting with, because that year functions as a kind of inflection point. Not the beginning of the practice, obviously. States have been hunting exiles since there were states and exiles. But 2013 is where the database shows the behavior consolidating into something more systematic, more normalized, and critically, more digitally enabled than what came before.

China leads the count by volume and geographic reach. Russia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and a spread of post-Soviet and African states fill out the list. Twenty-three governments in total, which represents a meaningful expansion from earlier reporting periods. The OHCHR has documented the underlying dynamic pretty clearly: globalization and digital technology have been steadily eroding whatever protection physical distance used to offer. You can flee a country. You cannot necessarily flee its surveillance apparatus anymore, not if that apparatus is resourced and motivated enough.

The digital piece is where 2013 gets specifically interesting. Spyware deployment, social media monitoring, coordinated online harassment against diaspora communities. These aren't just supplements to the old toolkit of physical intimidation and legal harassment. They're force multipliers. And the thing that made 2013 distinct from, say, 2003 is the commercial surveillance market. Sophisticated digital monitoring technology became available to states that previously lacked the in-house technical capacity to run comprehensive diaspora surveillance programs. You no longer needed a legacy KGB infrastructure to build a functional surveillance operation against your exiles. You could buy significant portions of that capability off the shelf.

The Interpol Red Notice abuse documented across the 23-government dataset is its own category of cynical. The Human Rights Foundation has tracked how this works in practice: a state files politically motivated criminal charges against an exile. Those charges generate an Interpol notice. The notice then functions as a tool of transnational harassment that is formally laundered through an international institution. The exile is now, on paper, a criminal suspect rather than a political refugee. Host country authorities receive that signal. Movement becomes restricted. Extradition pressure becomes plausible. The domestic repression has been successfully internationalized using the international community's own machinery.

Democratic host states come out of the Freedom House data looking genuinely unprepared for this. The FBI has documented Chinese, Russian, and Iranian "secret police station" operations inside the United States. Covert surveillance. Direct harassment of diaspora communities on American soil. The Council on Foreign Relations has noted that democracies have developed coordinated responses to transnational repression, but that those responses remain insufficient relative to the scale and sophistication of what they're countering. Systematic protection gaps is the polite way to put it. People at serious risk are falling through them.

None of this is abstract. The 2013 data captures real incidents: physical attacks, family member targeting (a particularly ugly coercion method, going after relatives still inside the country to pressure the exile), legal coercion, and digital surveillance, all deployed by governments that had made a strategic decision that exile was not a safe exit. The scale documented in that single year's data reflects not a collection of isolated cases but a governance tool that 23 different governments had independently concluded was worth deploying systematically.

That number, 23, is the thing to hold onto. This is not a handful of rogue states running idiosyncratic programs. By 2013, transnational repression had become common enough to document across two dozen governments in a single reporting year, with China at the front of the list but plenty of company behind it. The normalization question is the one that matters most for what comes after 2013, and the trajectory in subsequent years answers it pretty decisively.

text:
NEWS: Maryland family lawyers say AI is increasingly becoming a “second opinion” in divorce, custody and support cases — sometimes with expensive consequences. (Daily Record)

One attorney described a client who rejected a settlement after ChatGPT suggested she could receive far more. The original offer was withdrawn, the case moved toward trial, legal fees increased, and the client ultimately settled for less than the initial offer. 

Lawyers also say clients are getting tripped up by generic answers that don’t match Maryland law — including assumptions that marital property is automatically split 50-50, that fathers automatically receive equal custody, or that certain use-and-possession rights apply when they do not. 

Attorneys aren’t uniformly anti-AI. Some say it can help with basic definitions, research starting points and draft review. But they warn against uploading sensitive family-law documents or relying on AI for case-specific legal strategy because confidentiality, discovery and accuracy problems can follow.

text:
A young Madonna in 1977 smiling from the window of a car as she leaves Michigan for New York... 

Before she became a pop star, Madonna Louise Ciccone was a dance student in Michigan. Christopher Flynn, her ballet teacher, recognized her ambition and encouraged her to pursue a career beyond the state. She moved to New York as a teenager, intending to make her name as a dancer.

The city offered opportunity, but no guarantee of success. Madonna studied dance, auditioned and took jobs while finding her place in New York’s music and art scenes. She performed with the Breakfast Club and later formed Emmy before striking out on her own. In 1982, she released her first single, “Everybody.” Her self-titled debut album followed in 1983.

Flynn’s influence extended beyond dance. Madonna later recalled that he was one of the first people to make her feel valued as an artist. He also introduced her to Detroit’s gay nightlife, where she encountered the freedom and self-expression that would become central to her work.

The young woman in this photograph could not have known how far her career would go. Within a few years, she had moved from dance classes and small clubs to records heard around the world.

In a 2019 speech, Madonna credited Flynn with taking her to her first gay club and helping her feel that it was OK to be different.

text:
16-Year-Old Ilorin Robotics Prodigy Meets Governor’s Aide Following Viral InsideIlorin Spotlight

In a clear demonstration of Kwara State's open-door policy and commitment to youth-driven technology, the Senior Special Assistant to the Governor on Digital Innovations, Hon. Kayode Ishola @kaybabaofficial , hosted 16-year-old Ilorin-born robotics developer, Habibullah Yunus Shittu, in his office on Tuesday, September 22, 2026.

The reception was sparked by a viral video spotlighted by InsideIlorin on X (formerly Twitter) over the weekend. The footage showcased Habibullah’s project under his startup, Shelby Robotics, a fully functional, web-controlled restaurant robot designed to automate basic hospitality operations such as taking orders and transporting items across distances.

Habibullah’s invention seamlessly integrates electronics, robotics engineering, software development, and web technology. Uniquely engineered to bypass manual button controls, the robot is operated remotely via a custom web platform accessible through any smartphone or computer.

Outlining his long-term ambition during the visit, Habibullah said: "My goal is to keep improving this technology and eventually develop advanced robots capable of solving complex challenges across various industries."

Welcoming the young developer, Hon. Kayode Ishola underscored the administration’s focus on fostering local genius and creating direct channels between young innovators and state leadership.

"Your video went viral on Sunday, and by Tuesday, you are here presenting your project to a government official. This swift engagement clearly demonstrates that Kwara State Government, under Governor AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq CON, is deeply invested in home-grown innovations and remains accessible to young creators," Hon. Kayode stated.

"His Excellency has consistently prioritized human capital development and tech infrastructure, from establishing the Ilorin Innovation Hub to championing the Kwara Coding and Digital Literacy Programme across public schools, among other interventions."

Challenging the teenager to scale his concept, the Governor's aide offered strategic counsel: "Think beyond restaurant automation. Consider the broader applications for organizations and individuals requiring smart automation systems. Focus your next phase of development on three core pillars: durability, affordability, and a robust support system."

As a key takeaway from the interaction, Hon. Kayode announced that Habibullah will present his prototype at the upcoming Kwara Coding and Digital Literacy Programme Exhibition.

"You will have the privilege of showcasing Shelby Robotics to top government officials in Nigeria and potential private investors at the state exhibition," Hon. Kayode added.

The swift government intervention highlights Kwara State’s expanding ecosystem as a rising tech hub in Nigeria, propelled by accessible governance, targeted digital infrastructure, and active recognition of indigenous talent.

text:
Long Tweet

We're going into Week 3 so yes, I know it's extremely early for Off-Season talk so please spare me the "dude can we let the season play out," stuff....I know. I'm just looking and figured I would share. 

Here's some info about what the 2027 Free Agent class could look like ---->

RB -
There's a nice group of young backs that would basically fall into the same category of Jaylen Wright and Ollie Gordon. Basically meaning they're intriguing, young, and have flashed in limited time but have been stuck behind bigger names that dominate carries. Sean Tucker, Tyjae Spears, Roschon Johnson, Kendre Miller, Kimani Vidal.

WR's -

Puka Nacua, George Pickens, Rashee Rice, and Parker Washington. That's a group that I HIGHLY expect to end up re-signing with their current teams or will just be too big of an investment for Miami to be interested.

Then there's Tank Dell, Marvin Mims, Kayshon Boutte, Josh Downs, and Tre Tucker. That's a group, depending on how things play out this year, that could be intriguing to Miami.

TE -

The Lions crushed their 2023 draft class and when you do that you then have a bunch of guys to pay all roughly around the same time. In the last 11 months they've paid Jahmyr Gibbs, Aiden Hutchinson, and Jack Campbell. 

This upcoming spring they'll have to make decisions on Sam Laporta and Brian Branch. I'm not holding my breath, but I'm praying Sam Laporta(and/or Branch) makes it to Free Agency. Laporta is one of my favorite possibilities of next Off-Season, even if chances are low. He'll be 26 for large chunk of the season and would be worth the investment, IMO.

As for the remaining guys on the market, there's a bunch of names you'll be familiar with like TJ Hockenson, Evan Engram, Dallas Goedert, Jonnu Smith, and David Njoku. All of whom will be 30+ years old. The only other names that are semi-intriguing outside of Laporta because of their age + price tag + fit  combination are Colby Parkinson, who will be 28 going on 29, and a familiar face to Sully, current GB Packers' Luke Musgrave.

OL -

There's a ton of potential Free Agent OL that are under 30 years old. We'll see if Miami moves Proctor to RT or decides they like him too much at LG, but there will be plenty of choices available regardless of what their needs and open positions are. (Too many to list)

Edge -

Like Hafley said in one of his press availabilities, good ones really don't hit the market and become available very often.

Byron Young, Kayvon Thibodeaux, Dorance Armstrong, Tuli Tuipulotu, Jermaine Johnson, Yaya Diaby, Myles Murphy. According to spotrac, that's the list of pass rushers with a current potential AAV Market Value of $10Mil+.

Then, there's the rest, who are mostly retreads, some older, some still young; Kingsley Enagbare, Derek Barnett, Andrew Van Ginkel, Khalil Mack, Uchenna Nwosu, Malcolm Koonce, K'Lavon Chaisson, Baron Browning, Zaven Collins, Tyree Wilson, etc.

The Packers drafted Rashan Gary(1st) and Lukas Van Ness(1st), traded for Micah Parsons(gave up multiple 1st's), and signed Za'Darius and Preston Smith to big money deals in 2019. That's a pretty good track record which gives me confidence and some comfort that despite pass rush being non-existent this year it'll get figured out sooner than later.  I absolutely expect Sully to make a significant investment one way or another at that position, but the player must be deemed "worth it." 

DT -

The only interior DL predicted to have a significantly high market price is current LAR Kobie Turner. Other than that, it's full of older vets that are on the back half of the back 9 of their careers. Miami has youth at the position so although the market doesn't seem to have a ton to offer, it may not matter all that much if Miami chooses to continue to invest time into their current young guys.

LB -

Another position with a modest market(at best), offering mostly depth.  Miami already has a nice group that would lead you to believe they probably won't be very interested in adding much here.

CB -

The Packers have really never invested heavily at CB aside from Jaire Alexander being a 1st Round pick. With JuJu being the oldest of Miami's talented but young top 3, their focus and strategy could be more focused on improving the pass rush and helping the secondary in a roundabout way.

SAF -

There's a solid group there with familiar names.  Miami's unit has surprised so far and appear to have at least two legitimate players in Taaffe and Trader.  

Safety is a position we've seen the Packers attack and spend on going back to the Charles Woodson days when he converted from CB and as recent as a couple years ago when they made Xavier McKinney the highest paid safety at that time.

Jessie Bates, Jeremy Chinn, Brian Branch, Brandon Jones, Jaquan Brisker, Dax Hill, Xavier Woods, and plenty more.  

A ton of these guys, from all positions, are good players and will sign contracts with their current team so the market won't look at fruitful when the new league year rolls around again in March.

But, I'm a fan just like the rest of you and it's fun to look at the possibilities and hope certain guys don't return and become available.

For me though, I can't help but dream about landing Brian Branch and/or Sam Laporta.  I was in love with the Lions draft while it seemed like most were not fans.  

Long ways away and a lot is going to happen over the next couple months that we can't predict and it'll completely change what we're thinking we know now. 

Fingers crossed.

From 1932 to 1972, the U.S. Public Health Service conducted a study involving Black men in Alabama.
There were initially 600 participants: 399 with syphilis and 201 without it.
Researchers did not obtain informed consent.
The men were not told they were participating in a study designed to observe untreated syphilis. They were told they were being treated for “bad blood.”  
When penicillin became the established treatment for syphilis, researchers did not offer it to the men as treatment and allowed the study to continue.

text:
When I was 17 my mom decided she was retiring and moving across the country to Arizona, so she could be with the first grandchild in the fam. That left me with, essentially, nowhere to go.

I couch surfed for a while, got and lost jobs due to my deep depression (which had started in late hs), and eventually figured my shit out. Got my own place with a decent full time job. Enrolled in college. Became a volunteer EMT trainee. Joined the military.

I remember my dad being so angry at my mom (they had never been married) for “abandoning” me. It was weird because they usually agreed on parenting and showed immense respect for one another. But I think it was projection to a point.

His home wasn’t a safe place for me to live and he knew that. But he and my stepmom helped me out financially when they could.

Even then, still a mostly a kid, I wasn’t really mad at my mother. She spent 18 years raising me and 18 years before that raising my siblings. By herself, mostly, because her first husband was a deadbeat and my dad was an addict who did his best but often fell short. After all that time, plus running a daycare for 16 years, she deserved a break.

And I needed to be forced to get my shit together. I would have made her life miserable, I would have been stagnant and miserable, and nobody would have won.

All this to say that there is a difference between support and coddling. I think my mother, who did offer for me to move with her, would have inadvertently coddled me more. My dad wasn’t really that type of parent, for better or worse.

I survived. I thrived. And I NEEDED THAT. I needed to know I could take care of myself.

Taking care of yourself is scary!! It’s hard, at first. But it’s necessary to learn.

“I don’t want Siddhis, I don’t want wealth, I don’t want power, I don’t want health. Satgurudeva, I only want Your lotus feet upon my head.”
|| Na chahe mann siddhi, na chahe samriddhi. Na shakti, nahi arogya dhan sampada. Mathe rakhe Gurudeva Sri Charan kamalarvinda ||
This was the constant prayer of Lahiri Mahasya towards his Sri Guru, Mahavatar Babaji. He wanted the unattainable. His goal was the impossible-to-reach kingdom of the SatGuru, to be in His service forever. This intense clarity made someone living an ordinary life into a great spiritual master. Nothing was left unfulfilled for the shishya. The Guru gave him control over all the forces of nature, nothing was Aprapya (unattainable) in the material or spiritual world. But the shishya was filled with wisdom and sharanagati, he wanted that which is eternally Aprapya, eternally out of reach, the lotus feet of the SatGuru Himself. Even the greatest saints worked so tremendously hard to attain His feet, don’t feel that one can just laze around and get ahead on the spiritual path. The yearning to get to Bhagavan should burn everything of the inside. Another saint used to describe the longing for Bhagavan as molten gold hot as lava coursing through his veins, making him unable to do anything except dissolve into that Great Love. They truly understood the longing of the atma. Because everything was offered to the feet of the SatGuru, with no expectation from Him, to give or take when it is His deep will to do so. Every day a bhakta should wake up and walk more strongly towards the aim to reach Sri Hari Narayan, the SatGuru’s infinite lotus feet. The longing for His feet should burn stronger today than yesterday. Make the Unattainable One unable to wait far away from you. Make the One who is above All wish to place His remembrance in your mind firmly and never remove it. You can achieve it if you set your mind to it. Then, with His grace and your firm aim, even if any difficulties or obstacles come, you will cross them like it’s nothing.

text:
President Xi Jinping left Beijing on the afternoon of September 23.

After crossing the Pacific, he landed outside Washington, also on the afternoon of September 23.

By the clock, it almost seemed as though no time had passed. There is something strangely appropriate about that image. China and the United States today often appear extraordinarily far apart. Yet neither country is ever truly distant from the other.

And before Xi had even begun his meetings in Washington, something unusual happened.

President Trump, who just returned from NYC on the mid-night, did not wait for Xi at the White House. He went to Joint Base Andrews himself.

For a sitting US president, personally greeting a visiting foreign leader at the airfield is a rare gesture rather than a routine matter of protocol. In the context of visits by Chinese leaders to the United States, it was unprecedented in history. And it marked only the second instance since JFK went to this airport in 1962 to receive British Prime Minister Harold Macmillan.

The symbolism was difficult to miss. Before the formal talks had even begun, Washington was already signaling that it attached considerable political importance to the visit and wanted to establish a positive atmosphere for the discussions ahead.

I also noticed a warm moment at the arrival ceremony: Peng raised her hand to indicate someone's height while speaking with Melania, and the two were smiling. I could not help wondering whether they might have been talking about Barron.

Xi, making his 11th visit to the United States in 41 years, issued a written statement upon arrival. To the best of my recollection, this was also the first time he had formally released such a statement in the United States. I have not yet found a full official English translation, so I translated the remarks myself and offer some analysis here.

Xi's remarks are italicized; key points are highlighted in bold; all other text reflects my own analysis.

--I am very pleased to pay a state visit to the United States of America at the invitation of President Trump. On behalf of the Chinese people, I would like to extend sincere greetings and best wishes to the American people.

China and the United States are both great countries, and the two peoples are both great peoples. The two peoples have maintained friendly exchanges for a long time and their interests are deeply intertwined. China and the United States should be partners, not rivals. The great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again can go hand in hand. The two countries are not mutually exclusive, can help each other succeed and advance the well-being of the whole world.

The history of direct China-US engagement can be traced back to 1784. At the time, with American trade still constrained by Britain, US merchants decided to sail directly to China. Their ship, the Empress of China, eventually arrived in Guangzhou and was warmly received. Chinese and American accounts from the period contain strikingly positive descriptions of the other side. For more details, see the earlier post I shared in the comments.

Chinese thought, especially the teachings of Confucius, was valued by many of America's founding generation, including Franklin, Jefferson and Adams. Confucius is even depicted on the pediment of the US Supreme Court, a reminder of the intellectual curiosity with which some early Americans viewed Chinese civilization.

Chinese laborers played a crucial role in building the transcontinental railroad across the United States, a project that would have been extraordinarily difficult without them. 

Since the nineteenth century, American universities have helped educate generations of Chinese students. Tsinghua University, sometimes described as "China's MIT," was established with important American involvement through the Boxer Indemnity scholarship program, while Yenching University, one of the institutions that later contributed to the development of Peking University, dubbed "China's Harvard," was founded with substantial American support.

During World War II, China and the United States fought on the same side against fascism. In the later decades of the Cold War, the two countries again found significant strategic common ground.

Since China's reform and opening in 1978, China has supplied American consumers with vast quantities of affordable, high-quality goods, while many US companies have achieved remarkable commercial success in China, some on a scale they had never reached in their home market. China, in turn, benefited from access to American technology, capital, management practices, etc.

The point is not that the relationship has ever been free of conflict. It has not. The point is that competition and cooperation have coexisted in it almost from the beginning.

The phrase "the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and MAGA can go hand in hand" is striking because it deliberately adopts Trump's own political language.

Beijing is straightforward: China's rise does not have to come at the expense of America's decline, and no need for the United States to contain China.

It also carries an implicit message: China is not asking the United States to abandon its own national ambitions; by the same token, Washington should not automatically treat China's pursuit of a better life as a threat.

The formulation also leaves room for future deals:
If both sides can accept the premise that both countries can succeed, then issues such as trade, investment, technology, energy, and agriculture can, at least in principle, can be treated as matters of bargaining, exchange, and negotiated interests rather than as existential conflicts.

The most important sentence in Xi's statement, comes in the second paragraph: "China and the United States should be partners, not rivals." Xi has made this point to the US many times before. What is different this time is that he appears to have offered a more concrete framework for what that partnership could mean. Now look at the third paragraph:

--This year is a critical one for the development of both China and the United States. During President Trump's visit to China in May, we agreed to build a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability, providing strategic guidance for the future development of bilateral ties. China and the United States should work in the same direction, promote a stable relationship in which cooperation remains the mainstay, competition stays within bounds, differences remain manageable, and peace remains within reach. China and the United States, as two major countries, should find a right way to get along in the new era. I am confident that we can achieve this.

Notice what Xi is not saying.

The statement is not pretending that China-US competition can disappear. It is not asking Washington to abandon competition.

The real emphasis is on placing limits around that competition.

Competition may continue, but it should have boundaries.
Differences may persist, but they should remain controllable.
Neither side has to give up its ambitions, but neither should define the other's success as its own defeat.

That is the framework Beijing appears to be putting on the table, and clearly, the framework agreed upon at the Beijing meeting in May should now move from principle to further implementation.

--The world is developing and times are changing, but the historical logic of peaceful coexistence between China and the United States has not changed, the goodwill of friendly exchanges between the two peoples has not changed, and the general expectations of the international community for China and the United States have not changed.
I look forward to having in-depth exchanges with Trump on major issues concerning bilateral relations and the world situation, constantly enriching the connotation of the constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability, and expanding the space for exchanges and cooperation in various fields between the two countries.
I also looks forward to engaging extensively with people from all walks of life in the United States to deepen friendship.
With joint efforts, I believe the visit is sure to be fruitful, and will enhance the well-being of the two peoples and add hope for world peace.

The three things that have not changed underscore a broader point: whatever changes may occur in the international environment, China and the United States should not decouple to the point of outright hostility. Xi's reference to maintaining broad contacts with people from all walks of life in the United States and deepening friendship suggests a willingness to engage not only with federal officials, but also with the business community, academia, and the general public.

This is also consistent with how Xi has approached the United States in the past. When he visited as vice president, he made a point of returning to the small town in Iowa he had first visited as a young official and meeting old friends there. In 2015, he presented a medal to an American veteran who bravely flew missions over the Hump during WWII, and over the years he has repeatedly met with members of the American business and academic communities. More recently, he just wrote back to a group of young Americans.

If I had to reduce the entire speech to a single sentence, I would put it this way:

Beijing is trying to move the China-US relationship away from a framework of strategic confrontation and unlimited competition, and toward one in which competition remains possible but bounded, differences remain real but manageable, the overall relationship remains stable, and cooperation continues to occupy a meaningful place.

That, in my view, may be the most important test of this visit: whether competition can remain bounded without coming to define the entire relationship.

text:
Somaliland’s strategic position on the Gulf of Aden, just south of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, is giving new momentum to its decades-long campaign for international recognition, according to an analysis published by Foreign Policy on September 23.

In an article titled “The Iran War Might Be Somaliland’s Chance for Recognition,” journalist Joshua Keating reports that President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi “Irro” is seeking deeper U.S. engagement,and ultimately recognition, by highlighting #Somaliland’s strategic location, democratic record, relative stability and potential role in Red Sea security.

Speaking directly to Foreign Policy during his visit to Washington, President Irro said Somaliland had warned for years about the strategic importance of the region:

“We have been preaching for a long time that this area is very important to the world, to trade, to maritime security.”

President Irro said Somaliland had repeatedly offered to cooperate with international partners on maritime security but had often been overlooked in discussions concerning the Red Sea.

“For a long time, we’ve been offering a partnership on marine security.”

The President added that excluding Somaliland from the strategic calculations surrounding the Red Sea had been “a very serious mistake,” telling Foreign Policy that the deteriorating regional security environment had now reached “a boiling point.”

Foreign Policy also highlights Somaliland’s expanding international relationships, particularly its partnership with #Taiwan and Israel’s recognition of Somaliland. The report says maritime security has become an increasingly important part of Hargeisa’s case to Washington as developments involving the Houthis and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait heighten concerns over one of the world’s most important maritime trade routes.

President Irro also spoke positively about #US President Donald Trump and expressed hope that Somaliland’s message would reach him:

“President Trump is a great leader, and he’s trying to make peace.”

President Irro added: “Hopefully, our message directly reaches the president, and we hope he will respond positively.”

The report details Somaliland’s recent diplomatic push in Washington, including Irro’s meetings with members of Congress and U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for African Affairs Frank Garcia. Somaliland has presented itself as a stable security partner with experience confronting piracy and extremist threats, while supporters in Congress have pushed for greater economic engagement, including access to the SWIFT international financial messaging system.

On Somaliland’s relationship with Taiwan and the possibility of Washington adopting a different diplomatic approach toward Hargeisa without immediately granting full recognition, President Irro told Foreign Policy:

“We would welcome at least getting a different status than Somalia from the United States, especially status like Taiwan.”

He added: “They can deal the same way with Somaliland.”

The article also examines Somaliland’s relationship with Israel. President Irro said that in May 2025 he had appealed to governments around the world—including Arab states—to recognize Somaliland and that Israel was the only country to respond positively. 

Referring to the possibility of others following Israel, the President said “Hopefully, the others will follow.”

Foreign Policy concludes that it remains uncertain whether Somaliland’s growing strategic importance in the Red Sea, its relationships with Israel and Taiwan, and its expanding engagement in Washington will be enough to overcome longstanding international resistance to recognition.

President Irro, however, presented Somaliland’s 35-year pursuit of recognition in longer historical terms:

“We’ve learned a lot over the last 35 years. We are survivors.”

He called the structures "terrific." Then he said they need help. Then he said Washington offered to fund solutions. Then he said Pretoria ignored the offer.

Think about what that sequence means. A foreign ambassador toured a civil society security operation, praised it, offered money to expand it, and publicly complained that the host government would not cooperate.

That is not diplomacy. That is a shadow state inspection.

​​AfriForum's pitch is clever.​​

They submitted a Public Community Partnership proposal: fold the 178 watches into formal cooperation with SAPS and private security. Kallie Kriel said a positive response would address both local crime and US concerns.

Read that carefully. AfriForum is not asking for permission. It is offering a deal: let us in, and your diplomatic problem shrinks.

The subtext is unmistakable: reject us, and we can point to Washington and say "see, even the Americans think you are wrong."

​​The uncomfortable truth underneath.​​

Farm attacks are real. They are brutal. A subset involves torture and extreme violence that most South Africans never see because it happens on isolated properties far from cameras and witnesses.

Community watches grew because state response was inadequate. That is not an AfriForum claim. It is an observable fact. If SAPS rural response were adequate, there would be no market for private drone networks and farm watch control rooms.

But here is what the Bozell visit does not address:

AfriForum's watches cover a fraction of rural properties – disproportionately white-owned commercial farms. The vast majority of rural South Africans – farm workers, seasonal laborers, informal settlement residents – are not in AfriForum's coverage area. They do not have drones. They do not have cameras. They do not have an ambassador visiting their security situation.

​​The diplomatic function is the real story.​​

This visit is not about rural safety. It is about leverage.

Bozell has five asks. This is one of them. By touring AfriForum, praising its work, and offering US funding, he is creating a paper trail: we offered. They refused. The Americans had a solution and Pretoria said no.

That narrative is more valuable to Washington than any actual reduction in farm attacks.

​​Why Ramaphosa cannot say yes.​​

If he accepts the partnership, he validates AfriForum as a co-equal security provider – and implicitly acknowledges state failure. He also opens the door for US funding to flow through a politically active civil society organization, which carries its own sovereignty concerns.

If he refuses, Bozell cites the refusal as proof of indifference to rural violence.

It is a trap by design.

​​The final layer.​​

SAPS has its own rural safety challenges. Under-resourced. Under-stretched. Farm attacks are a small share of the overall murder total, but the brutality is distinctive and the isolation makes prevention nearly impossible without cooperation from landowners and communities.

AfriForum has capacity. SAPS has mandate. Neither trusts the other enough to integrate.

Bozell knows this. His visit did not solve it. It made the gap more visible.

A foreign ambassador touring a private security apparatus and offering to fund it while the host government looks on is not partnership.

It is a verdict.

text:
September 25 —
this year again,
I’ll savor the moon
while eating dango 🍡

On autumn nights in Japan,
people look up and say,
quite seriously,
that a rabbit is pounding rice cakes
on the moon.

Tonight I want to tell you why.

A thousand years ago,
Heian nobles did not merely glance
at the harvest moon.

They set silver grass in the garden,
offered round dumplings,
and sat in silence.

Wars came.
Plagues came.
Lives were short.

The moon was the one thing
that promised to return.

The fifteenth night
is the 15th day of the eighth lunar month —
not always the astronomical full moon.

This year they miss each other
by two days.

The Japanese do not call that a failure.
They smile and say,
“The famous moon is not necessarily full,”
and still they line up the dango.

Perfection is not required.
Looking is enough.

Ask a child what lives on the moon
and the answer is almost always
“a rabbit.”

The dark patches become a rabbit with a mallet,
pounding mochi forever.

Tell a friend abroad and they laugh:
“A rabbit? I thought it was cheese.”

We laugh too.

Then a parent strokes a child’s hair
and thinks, quietly:
may this same moon rise for you
when you are grown.

The dumplings are round.
The moon is round.
A family, if we are lucky,
is also round.

Even when it is not,
it waxes again.

So if the sky is cloudy tonight,
eat one dumpling for yourself.

Somewhere far away,
someone else is looking
at the same light.

Chūshū no Meigetsu
is not a festival that waits
for a perfect full moon.

It is the art of loving
what is incomplete —
and still calling it beautiful.

May it be a good night.🌕✨

A veiled threat implies harm without stating it directly, and law enforcement treats these hidden or indirect messages as serious criminal offenses if they cause sustained fear or intent to harm.
Understanding Veiled Threats
Definition: A veiled (or implied) threat uses code words, symbols, conditional phrasing, or subtle hints to suggest violence or negative consequences without making an overt declaration.
Legal Status: Courts evaluate the context, history between parties, and whether a reasonable person would perceive the message as a genuine threat.
First Amendment Limits: "True threats"—even when indirect, coded, or directed at law enforcement—are not protected speech under the First Amendment.
How Law Enforcement Handles Them
Digital Investigation: Officers and federal agencies use digital forensics and subpoenas to trace electronic messages, emails, and social media posts.
Context and Pattern: Investigators look at a "history of behavior" or prior interactions to decode implied coercion.
Actionable Reporting: Law enforcement advises victims to save all original evidence, take screenshots, and avoid replying to the sender before filing a formal report.

What is the significance of Judas betraying Jesus with a kiss?
Answer

Judas Iscariot was one of the original twelve disciples who followed and were taught by Jesus. Being in Jesus’ “inner circle,” Judas had a closer relationship to Jesus than most people during His ministry. Judas betrayed the Lord to the Jewish authorities. The pre-arranged signal was that the person Judas kissed was to be arrested and taken away (Mark 14:44). In this way the Son of Man was betrayed with a kiss (Luke 22:48).

In the culture of first-century Israel, a kiss was not always a romantic expression of love; rather, a kiss on the cheek was a common greeting, a sign of deep respect, honor, and brotherly love (see Luke 7:45; Romans 16:16; 1 Corinthians 16:20; 2 Corinthians 13:12; 1 Thessalonians 5:26; 1 Peter 5:14). For a student who had great respect for his teacher, a kiss fell well within the healthy expression of honor.

What really stands out in the mode of Judas’s betrayal is that Judas used such an intimate expression of love and respect to betray Jesus. Judas’s actions were hypocritical in the extreme—his actions said, “I respect and honor you,” at the exact time he was betraying Jesus to be murdered. Judas’s actions illustrate Proverbs 27:6, “Wounds from a friend can be trusted, but an enemy multiplies kisses.” Often, foes disguise themselves as friends. Evil often wears a mask to conceal its true purpose.
