Address by the President of the Governorate
Your Excellency Archbishop LUIGI Renna,

Distinguished Representatives of the Regional and Municipal Institutions,

Your Excellencies,
Distinguished Religious, Civil and Military Authorities,

Dear Guests,
First of all, I wish to express my heartfelt gratitude for the warm welcome extended to me and to the delegation of the Governorate of Vatican City State present here today, as well as for your numerous and heartfelt participation.

The Ninth Centenary of the Translation of the Relics of Saint Agatha is an occasion of the highest significance, in which profound faith, centuries-old devotion to the sacred remains of the Saint, and artistic endeavor—understood in its noblest sense as an instrument of evangelization—come together in one solemn celebration.

The Governorate, which I have the honor to represent, has followed every delicate stage of the restoration of the reliquary bust and the precious Veil with deep devotion and the utmost professional care. This work of extraordinary complexity was entrusted to the outstanding specialist team of the Directorate of Museums and Cultural Heritage, led with dedication and exemplary expertise by Barbara Pinto Folicaldi.

We are fully aware of what Saint Agatha represents for this community. She is not merely its Patron Saint; she is its Mother, its faithful Guardian, its Protectress, to whom the people turn in times of trial. Throughout the centuries, the people of Catania have always gathered around "their" Saint whenever adversity struck. The bond between this fearless witness to Christ—a young woman of unwavering faith, even to the supreme sacrifice of her life—and her faithful remains unbreakable.

For this reason, the conservation work takes on a significance that transcends its purely artistic and technical dimension, touching the deepest chords of spirituality and collective identity. Restoring the original splendor of the sacred reliquary that safeguards the Saint's relics is, in itself, an act of veneration and profound homage to her martyrdom.

Aware that transferring both the reliquary and the relics outside the Cathedral would have involved considerable logistical challenges, we deemed it appropriate to carry out the restoration on site. Thus, the reliquary bust—a masterpiece of fourteenth-century goldsmith's art—was restored within the Archbishop's Palace, in the heart of Catania.

Commissioned in 1376 by Bishop Marziale to the renowned goldsmith Giovanni di Bartolo, the gilded silver bust houses the sacred skull of the Virgin Martyr. The work portrays Saint Agatha flanked by two angels, presenting her with a serene countenance made even more gentle by the rediscovery of its original polychromy.

Over the centuries, popular devotion enriched the sacred image with a remarkable and layered collection of ex-voto offerings. Precious necklaces, gold pendants, enamel ornaments, pearls, brooches, and medallions were removed with the utmost care from the repoussé and chased silver surface. Each jewel was then meticulously catalogued and repositioned on a specially designed bodice fitted to a faithful three-dimensional replica of the reliquary.

Every stage of the restoration was preceded by thorough diagnostic investigations conducted by the Scientific Research Laboratory of the Vatican Museums. The structural and aesthetic conservation work was carried out by the Vatican Museums' Metals and Ceramics Restoration Laboratory, while the Veil—another fundamental object of devotion—was entrusted to the Museums' Tapestries and Textiles Restoration Laboratory.

Thanks to the expert dedication of all the professionals involved and to the exemplary collaboration established between the Archdiocese of Catania and the Directorate of Museums and Cultural Heritage of the Governorate, the reliquary bust is today returned to the veneration of the faithful in the fullness of its original beauty.

On behalf of the Governorate of Vatican City State, I am very pleased to offer the Archdiocese and the entire community of Catania, especially in the period of this Jubilee, a renewed priceless artifact that safeguards the sacred memory of your territory: the living and enduring presence of Agatha, your beloved Patron Saint and a lasting symbol of unity, charity, fidelity, and hope.

Thank you.
Newly Restored Reliquary Bust and Veil of Saint Agatha is presented in Catania, Sicily

Urged by faith, we are obliged to believe and to maintain that the Church is one, holy, catholic, and also apostolic. We believe in her firmly and we confess with simplicity that outside of her there is neither salvation nor the remission of sins, as the Spouse in the Canticles [Sgs 6:8] proclaims: ‘One is my dove, my perfect one. She is the only one, the chosen of her who bore her,‘ and she represents one sole mystical body whose Head is Christ and the head of Christ is God [1 Cor 11:3]. In her then is one Lord, one faith, one baptism [Eph 4:5]. There had been at the time of the deluge only one ark of Noah, prefiguring the one Church, which ark, having been finished to a single cubit, had only one pilot and guide, i.e., Noah, and we read that, outside of this ark, all that subsisted on the earth was destroyed.
We venerate this Church as one, the Lord having said by the mouth of the prophet: ‘Deliver, O God, my soul from the sword and my only one from the hand of the dog.’ [Ps 21:20] He has prayed for his soul, that is for himself, heart and body; and this body, that is to say, the Church, He has called one because of the unity of the Spouse, of the faith, of the sacraments, and of the charity of the Church. This is the tunic of the Lord, the seamless tunic, which was not rent but which was cast by lot [Jn 19:23- 24]. Therefore, of the one and only Church there is one body and one head, not two heads like a monster; that is, Christ and the Vicar of Christ, Peter and the successor of Peter, since the Lord speaking to Peter Himself said: ‘Feed my sheep‘ [Jn 21:17], meaning, my sheep in general, not these, nor those in particular, whence we understand that He entrusted all to him [Peter]. Therefore, if the Greeks or others should say that they are not confided to Peter and to his successors, they must confess not being the sheep of Christ, since Our Lord says in John ‘there is one sheepfold and one shepherd.’ We are informed by the texts of the gospels that in this Church and in its power are two swords; namely, the spiritual and the temporal. For when the Apostles say: ‘Behold, here are two swords‘ [Lk 22:38] that is to say, in the Church, since the Apostles were speaking, the Lord did not reply that there were too many, but sufficient. Certainly the one who denies that the temporal sword is in the power of Peter has not listened well to the word of the Lord commanding: ‘Put up thy sword into thy scabbard‘ [Mt 26:52]. Therefore, both are in the power of the Church, namely, the spiritual sword and the material. But indeed, the latter is to be exercised on behalf of the Church; and truly, the former is to be exercised by the Church. The former is of the priest; the latter is by the hand of kings and soldiers, but at the will and sufferance of the priest.

However, one sword ought to be subordinated to the other and temporal authority, subjected to spiritual power. For since the Apostle said: ‘There is no power except from God and the things that are, are ordained of God‘ [Rom 13:1-2], but they would not be ordained if one sword were not subordinated to the other and if the inferior one, as it were, were not led upwards by the other.

For, according to the Blessed Dionysius, it is a law of the divinity that the lowest things reach the highest place by intermediaries. Then, according to the order of the universe, all things are not led back to order equally and immediately, but the lowest by the intermediary, and the inferior by the superior. Hence we must recognize the more clearly that spiritual power surpasses in dignity and in nobility any temporal power whatever, as spiritual things surpass the temporal. This we see very clearly also by the payment, benediction, and consecration of the tithes, but the acceptance of power itself and by the government even of things. For with truth as our witness, it belongs to spiritual power to establish the terrestrial power and to pass judgement if it has not been good. Thus is accomplished the prophecy of Jeremias concerning the Church and the ecclesiastical power: ‘Behold to-day I have placed you over nations, and over kingdoms‘ and the rest. Therefore, if the terrestrial power err, it will be judged by the spiritual power; but if a minor spiritual power err, it will be judged by a superior spiritual power; but if the highest power of all err, it can be judged only by God, and not by man, according to the testimony of the Apostle: ‘The spiritual man judgeth of all things and he himself is judged by no man‘ [1 Cor 2:15]. This authority, however, (though it has been given to man and is exercised by man), is not human but rather divine, granted to Peter by a divine word and reaffirmed to him (Peter) and his successors by the One Whom Peter confessed, the Lord saying to Peter himself, ‘Whatsoever you shall bind on earth, shall be bound also in Heaven‘ etc., [Mt 16:19]. Therefore whoever resists this power thus ordained by God, resists the ordinance of God [Rom 13:2], unless he invent like Manicheus two beginnings, which is false and judged by us heretical, since according to the testimony of Moses, it is not in the beginnings but in the beginning that God created heaven and earth [Gen 1:1]. Furthermore, we declare, we proclaim, we define that it is absolutely necessary for salvation that every human creature be subject to the Roman Pontiff.

text:
The Son is the center of the marriage because the Son is the center of everything God is doing. The Father has committed all judgment unto the Son, “That all men should honour the Son, even as they honour the Father” (John 5:22-23). The religious man wants God without the Son, morality without the blood, a kingdom without the King, and a wedding feast without the Bridegroom. That arrangement may satisfy an interfaith luncheon, but it will not survive the judgment of God. No man reaches the Father by avoiding Christ. No man enters God’s future by admiring Jesus as a teacher while rejecting Him as Lord and Saviour. The marriage glorifies the Son because redemption glorifies the Son. The nail-scarred Bridegroom will not stand unnoticed in a corner of His own wedding while human religion receives the applause.

The marriage also declares that God’s purpose ends in joy, fellowship, and triumph rather than permanent mourning. The Church has passed through persecution, bereavement, disappointment, weakness, and the long warfare of faith, but the Bride’s destination is not the furnace. Her destination is the Bridegroom. Paul wrote that Christ loved the Church “and gave himself for it; That he might sanctify and cleanse it with the washing of water by the word” and “present it to himself a glorious church” (Ephesians 5:25-27). Notice who performs the work. Christ loves, gives, sanctifies, cleanses, and presents. The Bride is not dragging herself into Heaven by the hem of her own religious garment. She is carried there by the saving purpose of the One who bought her. Grace does not merely rescue the sinner from Hell; it prepares a people for the Son.

2. The Invitation Israel Made Light Of

The king “sent forth his servants to call them that were bidden to the wedding: and they would not come” (Matthew 22:3). Those words summarize centuries of Israel’s resistance to God’s messengers. The nation possessed the covenants, the promises, the prophets, the law, the temple, and the expectation of Messiah. When the King arrived, religious leadership inspected Him with the enthusiasm of undertakers measuring a living man for a coffin. John the Baptist announced Him. The apostles preached Him. The miracles authenticated Him. The Scriptures identified Him. Yet the rulers preferred their position to their Messiah. Christ declared, “ye will not come to me, that ye might have life” (John 5:40). Their problem was not insufficient evidence. Their problem was an unwilling heart wearing a scholarly robe.

The king sent other servants, saying, “Behold, I have prepared my dinner: my oxen and my fatlings are killed, and all things are ready: come unto the marriage” (Matthew 22:4). Nothing remained for the invited guests to prepare. The king had supplied the feast. Their responsibility was to come at his call. Here the practical gospel application shines without erasing the passage’s Jewish setting. Calvary is finished. Christ did not die halfway, rise provisionally, and leave sinners to complete redemption with church membership, water baptism, sacraments, law-keeping, or improved manners. He cried, “It is finished” (John 19:30). Religion keeps bringing a lunch box to a banquet God has already furnished. It offers its stale crackers of human merit while the King announces that all things are ready. Salvation is received by faith because Christ has completed the work.

“But they made light of it, and went their ways, one to his farm, another to his merchandise” (Matthew 22:5). They were not all shouting atheists or sword-carrying persecutors. Some were simply too busy. The farm looked more important than the King, merchandise seemed more profitable than the marriage, and daily affairs smothered eternal truth beneath ordinary dust. Men still perish respectably. One does not have to curse Christ to reject Him; he can merely postpone Him until death removes the calendar. The man who laughs at the gospel and the man who is too occupied to consider it

text:
The first photos of the three Israeli "spies" arrested in Egypt
The Israeli newspaper *Yedioth Ahronoth* published photos of the three "spies" detained in Egypt; all of them belong to the Al-Azazmeh tribe from the Negev town of Segev Shalom.

The detainees are Bilal Masoudin (27, married with two children), Bilal Salem Abu Aish (28, married with five children), and Ahmed Al-Doji (25).

The Hebrew newspaper reported that the three men were apprehended by Egyptian General Intelligence at the Taba crossing on March 21, after being ordered to exit their taxi and transfer into Egyptian intelligence vehicles.

*Yedioth Ahronoth* stated that Egyptian authorities continue to withhold information regarding the fate of the three Negev Bedouin Israelis—who have been detained for six months—while Tel Aviv acknowledges its inability to obtain official details, offering only brief responses that leave the families in a state of growing anxiety.

The newspaper added that the families received messages indicating the detention was not due to a criminal offense, but rather matters concerning Egyptian national security.

It noted that the families had maintained media silence for months in hopes of the men's release, but all inquiries proved futile; even the Egyptian lawyers hired by the families resigned after failing to secure any information. Meanwhile, the Israeli Foreign Ministry, the Prime Minister's Office, and the President's Office have offered only terse replies, stating simply that they would provide updates the moment any new information became available. It was noted that former Knesset member Taleb a-Sana—a lawyer—was retained by the families to handle this obscure case. He contacted Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, President Isaac Herzog, and Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar, but received only brief responses stating that the matter was being addressed. He expressed frustration at the lack of a serious response, contrasting this with the immediate attention Israelis detained elsewhere in the world typically receive.

*Yedioth Ahronoth* reported that lawyer Yitzhak Meltzer, based in Be'er Sheva, also contacted relevant Israeli government ministries but failed to obtain answers. Meanwhile, Merav Marx, Director of the Diplomatic and Civil Law Department at the Foreign Ministry, stated that the ministry has been working with the relevant Egyptian authorities since March 21. She confirmed her understanding that the three men are in custody but noted that she lacks further information, despite numerous inquiries.

The Hebrew newspaper added that Israel’s Ambassador to Egypt, Ori Rotman—who is operating from Tel Aviv because his credentials have not yet received Egyptian approval—refused to comment on the detention case and referred the newspaper to the Foreign Ministry spokesperson. Meanwhile, former MK Taleb a-Sana, upon visiting the Egyptian Embassy in Tel Aviv and meeting directly with the Egyptian consul, found that the only response provided was that the three men were in custody.

It was further noted that the Israeli Foreign Ministry issued a statement confirming it is handling the case of three Israeli citizens in Egypt with whom contact has been lost. The ministry stated that it had submitted requests to Egyptian authorities for official information but had not yet received an adequate official response; it affirmed that it would continue to engage with Egyptian authorities and maintain contact with the families. Source: Yedioth Ahronoth

Penny Wong’s commitment to a two-state solution, and to the so-called Palestinian “right of return,” is more dangerous than you might think.

She and much of the Left keep selling the public a story about Palestinian nationalism that does not match what the movement itself says. They treat Hamas and the Palestinian Authority as if they were ordinary national movements looking for a state beside Israel. They are not.

The reason Palestinian leaders have rejected deal after deal, including offers that gave them almost everything they publicly demanded, is not a mystery. Hamas’s 1988 Charter says it outright. Article 11 treats the whole land as Islamic waqf: an endowment belonging to Allah, set aside for Muslims until Judgment Day. No Arab government, no Palestinian organisation, and no international body has the right to give any of it up. In that reading, the land is Dar al-Islam. It cannot be sold, partitioned, or handed to non-Muslims. Stewardship is allowed. Ownership by Jews is not. Selling land to Jews has been treated as betrayal, and Palestinian religious authorities have issued an automatic fatwa against anyone who tries and their family.

That is not a side slogan. It is a doctrine the Muslim Brotherhood and its offshoots take seriously. Hamas wrote it into its founding charter. The PA’s own clergy have used the same waqf language. In 2018 the PA Grand Mufti said Palestine, including Jerusalem, is waqf until Judgment Day and must not be relinquished to “enemies.” The 2026 PA draft constitution does not copy Hamas word for word, but it follows the same refusal. It calls Palestine part of the Arab homeland and the Palestinians part of the Arab nation. The parliament and the President himself, must swear to protect the country’s “national and pan-Arab components and heritage.” The PLO stays the supreme representative. The right of return is locked in. There is no recognition of Jewish sovereignty over any of the land.

So when Wong says Mahmoud Abbas made verbal commitments - recognise Israel, reform government, end pay-to-slay, change the schools, demilitarise, hold elections, keep Hamas out, she is presents press-conference promise as if it cancelled the doctrine. Abbas cannot deliver that. The movement made this claim religious so it would travel. That is why “Free Palestine” works as a global slogan far beyond the West Bank and Gaza. It is no longer presented as a border dispute. It is presented as sacred land that must be recovered.

League of Nations mandates, legal land purchases, and Israel’s independence may be valid in Western law. They are not valid under this claim. That is why partition plans from 1947 onward were rejected. The rejection is theological and political, not just tactical.

Hamas is not trying to build a small Palestinian state next to Israel. It is trying to keep the whole land inside an Islamic and Arab frame. The PA uses softer language and diplomatic costumes. The destination is the same: Israel as a Jewish state is illegitimate, and return is the tool that would undo it.

Wong ignores the Hamas Charter and the PA’s own texts, repeats the verbal pledges, keeps the victim story front and centre, and keeps the money flowing. That is not neutrality. It is an endorsement, made by a senior Australian Cabinet minister, of a Brotherhood-derived doctrine dressed up as ordinary state-building.

Captives of the Golden Sun – Part III • The Gilded Cage & The Broken Promise

The Story So Far (Part III. description)

In the summer of 1975, European travelers Ingrid and Lotte were lured into a carefully prepared trap by Samira, drugged, captured, and violently separated. Ingrid surrendered her freedom after Samira promised that her obedience would ensure Lotte’s safety. Unknown to her, Lotte was instead handed over to Samira’s brother Malik and taken across the desert as merchandise.

In Part II, Lotte endured an exhausting journey to the city, where she was prepared for auction and sold to a wealthy Sheikh. Meanwhile, Ingrid was transformed into Samira’s silent servant—dressed in gold, restrained, and forced to endure repeated humiliation in the belief that every act of obedience was protecting the woman she loved.

Part III follows their two distant paths as they continue to unfold beneath the same unforgiving sun.

Lotte is brought to the Sheikh’s home as an expensive gift for his wife, Nawal, whose fascination with women and control is immediately awakened by the silent European captive. Yet beneath Nawal’s dominant nature lies a capacity for compassion that Lotte has not encountered since her ordeal began. As she listens to Lotte’s story, improves the conditions of her confinement, and offers her protection, curiosity slowly develops into tenderness. Lotte remains restrained and far from free, but within this gilded cage she discovers the first fragile traces of safety—and perhaps the beginning of an unexpected bond.

Ingrid’s captivity follows a far darker course. Still believing in Samira’s promise, she submits to degrading service and bears every restraint with quiet dignity for Lotte’s sake. That sacrifice becomes meaningless when Samira returns with Malik and allows him to reveal the truth: Lotte was taken to the market and sold, while brother and sister shared the profit.

The revelation destroys Ingrid’s last reason to cooperate. Her grief soon hardens into open defiance, and she declares that Samira will never again receive her willing obedience. Deprived of the lie that once gave her power, Samira turns to force, leaving Ingrid bound in a cellar until thirst, exhaustion, and isolation can accomplish what deception no longer can.

Thus, the two women end this chapter farther apart than ever. Lotte’s captivity begins to soften under Nawal’s growing compassion, while Ingrid’s ordeal descends into an increasingly merciless struggle of wills. Neither knows where the other is, whether she is safe, or whether they will ever meet again—but even across the distance, their love remains the invisible force shaping every choice they make.

Their cages are different. Their futures remain uncertain. And their story is far from over.

The Visual Journey (Photo Descriptions)

1. After paying a considerable price for Lotte at the city slave market, the Sheikh brings her into his home as a living gift for his senior wife. He studies the silent, hollow-eyed young woman and wonders whether such a withdrawn captive was truly a wise investment. Lotte no longer weeps or resists; exhausted by all she has endured, she has retreated into lethargy, consumed above all by uncertainty over Ingrid’s fate.

2. Before leaving, the Sheikh orders one of his servants to give the parched Lotte water. His concern is partly pragmatic—she is an expensive possession intended for the woman he loves—but the servant’s response is genuinely compassionate. Lotte drinks eagerly and looks up at her with quiet gratitude, finding a first small trace of human kindness within the unfamiliar household.

3. The Sheikh proudly presents his costly gift to his senior wife, Nawal, knowing well of her attraction to submissive women and actively encouraging it. Lotte immediately captures Nawal’s curious attention, yet the young captive remains emotionally absent, overwhelmed by recent suffering and fear for the beloved Ingrid whose whereabouts she still does not know.

4. Having accepted Lotte as her new possession, Nawal leads her to a private wardrobe and invites her to choose from its elegant dresses. The offer creates a small illusion of choice, but Lotte gives no answer and shows no interest in the garments before her. Her silence reveals how far she has withdrawn from a world in which every meaningful decision has already been taken away.

5. Since Lotte will not choose, Nawal dresses her in a modest black ensemble selected according to her own taste. The heavy wooden pillory has finally been removed, but freedom lasts only briefly: Nawal now holds the iron restraints that will replace it. She is not driven by simple cruelty, yet her fascination with submissive women, possession and restraint is unmistakable—and she intends to exercise it upon her husband’s gift.

6. Moments later, Lotte stands before Nawal with iron cuffs locked around her wrists and ankles. The restraints are less brutal than the wooden pillory, but their weight and short chains still restrict every movement and clearly define her new position within the household. Nawal studies her with growing interest, while Lotte remains distant and resigned, physically present yet still searching inwardly for some sign of Ingrid.

7. The narrative now shifts to Ingrid, who remains captive within Samira’s residence. As Samira bids farewell to her guest Layla, Ingrid waits silently beside them, displayed in an exquisite robe, golden restraints and an ornate mask as proof of her captor’s triumph. For a woman once accustomed to commanding obedience, such decorative servitude is profoundly humiliating—and Samira understands this perfectly. Yet Ingrid endures it because she believes every act of compliance helps keep Lotte safe.

8. Once the guest has departed, the glittering performance ends and the raw reality of captivity returns. Samira takes Ingrid into a neglected storeroom and maliciously presents the plain, coarse dress that will replace her magnificent costume. The beautiful European trophy displayed before company is now reduced to an ordinary household captive.

9. Dressed in the simple garment, Ingrid sits against a wooden post while Samira finishes securing her with broad leather straps. Samira’s cruel satisfaction reveals how much she enjoys the helplessness of another dominant woman, especially one who might once have regarded herself as an equal. Ingrid meets the humiliation with outward calm, preserving her strength by thinking only of Lotte and the safety her obedience is supposed to guarantee.

10. Exhaustion eventually allows Ingrid to fall asleep despite the restrictive straps and hard cellar floor. A soft, almost blissful smile appears upon her face—the only happiness captivity has permitted her. It belongs not to the room around her, but to a fragile dream of Lotte and the life they once shared.

11. Morning brings heavier iron restraints and a new series of commands. Kneeling before Samira, Ingrid is made to raise her face and look directly into her captor’s eyes while the day’s duties are explained. She does not flinch or lower her gaze; her body obeys, but the proud Mistress within her remains carefully hidden and intact.

12. At breakfast, Samira cannot resist transforming an ordinary meal into another demonstration of hierarchy. She eats comfortably from a richly laid table while Ingrid, shackled at her feet, receives coarse food upon the floor. Ingrid accepts the indignity in silence, still believing that every humiliation endured may buy another measure of safety for Lotte.

13. Later, Samira relaxes with her water pipe while ordering Ingrid to polish her tall black boots. The reversal is deliberately chosen: the former Mistress now kneels in chains, tending the symbols of another woman’s authority. Samira watches with quiet satisfaction, while Ingrid performs the task without offering her the emotional surrender she seeks.

14. Samira’s next command turns Ingrid into an instrument of her comfort. As her captor reclines with a book, the shackled Ingrid kneels beside her and works a large hand fan. The duty appears almost peaceful, yet its stillness conceals the same calculated humiliation—Samira rests because the woman she has conquered must labor.

15. Before leaving for the city, Samira secures Ingrid against the wall with her wrists raised, ankles shackled and eyes covered by a broad leather blindfold. Dressed in her conservative black public robes, she offers an ironic farewell wave to a woman who cannot see it. Ingrid is left to wait in darkness, able to hear Samira depart but powerless to know when—or with whom—she will return.

16. For the last time in this part, the narrative returns to Lotte. Nawal orders her shackled captive to kneel, but instead of demanding service, she invites the previously silent woman to tell her story. As Nawal listens, her curiosity gives way to genuine sympathy: Lotte is slowly becoming more than a private plaything in her eyes—a wounded woman with a past, a lost love, and emotions of her own. Yet this awakening compassion has its limits, and Lotte’s restraints remain firmly in place.

17. The scene moves to the bath, where Nawal asks Lotte to wash her back. Lotte obeys, beginning to regard her new Mistress with cautious relief; although she remains confined, Nawal treats her with a decency she has not known during the brutal days since her capture.

18. After the bath, Nawal’s changing attitude becomes visible in a small but meaningful concession. She replaces Lotte’s heavy, uncomfortable irons with more elegant and comfortable restraints, personally fastening the ornate cuffs around her wrists and ankles. It is an act of consideration, though not freedom—Nawal softens the conditions of Lotte’s captivity without surrendering her control.

19. Lotte now faces her first test of life within the household: serving Nawal and the long-established women of the harem while still shackled. Concentrating intensely, she struggles with movements made awkward by her chains, while the other women laugh at the European newcomer’s clumsiness, forgetting how difficult their own beginnings once were. Amid their amusement, Nawal offers Lotte a quiet, encouraging gaze—as if promising that she will learn, adapt, and eventually find her place.

20. Later that evening, the Sheikh asks his wife whether she is satisfied with his costly gift and whether Lotte has shown proper obedience and respect. His presence deeply unsettles Lotte, reminding her of the auction, the brutal journey in the wooden pillory, and the men who have caused her so much suffering. Sensing her distress, Nawal draws her close with an arm around her shoulders—not as a gesture of possession, but of protection, silently assuring her that she is safe beside her.

21. At the end of the long day, Nawal gives Lotte a modest room of her own. The restraints remain, and a long chain secures her to the bed, but she is granted privacy and enough freedom of movement for her basic needs—a mercy far removed from the cold cellars and storerooms she has come to fear. As Nawal gently covers her with a blanket, kindness and the first trace of deeper attachment appear in her expression; Lotte responds with quiet gratitude, increasingly aware that her new Mistress may not be the monster she expected. Here we leave Lotte for now—but her story, and the strange bond beginning to form between these two women, is far from over.

22. For the last time in this part, the narrative returns to Ingrid. Samira arrives home from the city accompanied by her brother Malik—the man who secretly took Lotte to the slave auction despite Samira’s promise to keep her safe in exchange for Ingrid’s obedience. Still blindfolded and chained to the wall, Ingrid hears only approaching footsteps, laughter, and unfamiliar words, unaware that her fragile illusion of Lotte’s safety is about to be destroyed.

23. Once the blindfold is removed, Ingrid recognizes Malik as the man she briefly met during her last visit to Samira’s house with Lotte. She does not yet know what happened after their separation or the part he played in her beloved’s fate. Anticipating a violent reaction to the truth, Samira secures Ingrid’s wrists behind her back and binds her arms and body tightly with broad leather straps before allowing Malik to speak.

24. Malik now reveals everything: the journey to the city, the auction, and the wealthy Sheikh who purchased Lotte. With cruel pride, he empties the purse of gold he received onto the table, turning the price of Lotte’s suffering into a display of his own success. For the first time, Ingrid’s strength finally breaks; unable to bear the truth about the woman she loves, she sinks into helpless tears.

25. Bound tightly and emptied of resistance, Ingrid lies on the carpet while Samira and Malik divide the gold earned from Lotte’s sale. The image draws its cruelty from the stark contrast between Ingrid’s silent grief and the satisfied smiles of the siblings, who reduce another woman’s ruined life to neat stacks of shining coins.

26. Pleased with his profit, Malik takes his leave and shares an affectionate farewell with his sister. Samira keeps one hand firmly on Ingrid’s arm while watching him depart, but Ingrid barely reacts. The revelation has pushed her beyond tears into a state of numb resignation, her expression distant and extinguished.

27. Once Malik is gone, grief gives way to fury. Still bound and kneeling, Ingrid confronts Samira over her betrayal, denouncing the broken promise and declaring that she will never willingly serve, obey, or humble herself before her again. Samira remains outwardly calm, yet realizes that her most powerful weapon is gone: from now on, only physical restraints can hold Ingrid under her control.

28. Recovering quickly from this setback, Samira decides to force the obedience she can no longer obtain through deception. Ingrid is taken to a cellar storeroom and secured to a tall wooden cross, her outstretched wrists, body, and ankles held by strong leather straps while her feet remain on the floor. Samira makes her terms unmistakably clear—Ingrid will remain there until she capitulates and promises obedience—but Ingrid answers only with contemptuous silence.

29. Night settles over the storeroom, illuminated only by a pale shaft of moonlight entering through the small window. Exhaustion eventually pulls Ingrid into sleep, but there is no trace of the peaceful smile she wore the previous night. Her head hangs heavily and her rest is tormented by fear for Lotte, whose unknown fate now haunts even her dreams.

30. In the morning, Samira returns carrying a pitcher of water and offers Ingrid one final choice: submission in exchange for relief. Thirsty, exhausted, and soaked with perspiration, Ingrid nevertheless refuses with the same determined silence. Laughing at her defiance, Samira slowly pours the water onto the stone floor, allowing it to form a small pool before her helpless captive. Thus Part III closes with Ingrid’s fate as uncertain as Lotte’s—not with surrender, but with a silent and unresolved battle of wills.

Accord­ing to John Campea, this Reddit plot leak for Avengers: Doomsday is legit. Read it below and tell me what you think. SPOILERS BELOW.

(1/2)
Avengers: Doomsday opens in NYC on Tobey Maguire’s Spider-Man’s Earth. He’s fighting Deadpool and Wolverine, who were sent there with a planet-killing bomb built by Beast to destroy Tobey’s world in order to save their own universe from an Incursion. Tobey battles Hugh Jackman’s Wolverine, who manages to plant the device. Wolverine stays behind when it detonates, and both he and Tobey’s Spider-Man - along with everyone on that Earth - are killed. Deadpool escapes and returns to his own Earth, which we see in the distance. Charles Xavier watches the destroyed world below with sadness… but they had no choice.
We then cut to Tony’s funeral. Steve speaks with some of the heroes, including Ant-Man, before returning the Stones. He goes back in time and chooses to stay with Peggy. They have a son, Jim. One day, Loki visits them - this is before the Loki Season 2 finale. He tells Steve about the TVA and warns him that they will soon prune this timeline because Steve was never meant to live there or have a son. Loki offers them a way out: he can take them to a universe where they don’t exist and can live in peace - the Fantastic Four’s universe. Before leaving, Loki gives Steve a special card to contact him.
Steve and his family live there for ten years.
We then see Doctor Doom visiting Sue and Franklin. They clearly know each other. Doom says he has come to speak with Reed. He warns him about the Incursions and reveals their universe is next. He proposes a plan - but they must travel with him to Earth-616. Doom also asks Reed whether it’s possible someone from another universe is living in theirs. They scan the planet and discover an anomaly: Steve and his family.
They confront Steve, who recognizes them after living there for a decade. They explain the Incursions and ask him to come to 616 to help convince the Avengers to trust Doom’s plan. They travel there, and Steve successfully persuades the heroes to listen.
Next, they visit the X-Men’s universe - but the X-Men are hostile. They’ve survived multiple Incursions and trust no one. They assume the MCU heroes and the Fantastic Four have come to destroy them and attack.
Reed and Doom explains their solution: to build massive cannons on each Earth that will permanently separate the universes and stop the Incursions. They will split into teams and each one will go to another Earth to place a canon there.
Meanwhile, Steve tells Thor he met a Loki who is still alive. Thor asks Steve to take him to him. Using Loki’s card, they locate the TVA - but when they arrive, everyone is dead and Loki has had his heart ripped out. They realize Doom is responsible.
Steve goes back to confront Doom, who reveals his true plan: to allow the Incursions to happen so he can rebuild the Multiverse in his own image and resurrect his dead family. He takes Steve to his castle in Latveria on his Earth. There, Steve meets Doom’s followers - masked witches. One of them impersonates Peggy to manipulate him.
Doom reveals that Steve’s presence in their universe is what triggered their Incursion, because he didn’t belong there. It also led to the death of Doom’s family: Doom became obsessed with stopping the Incursion, conducting dangerous experiments - one of which failed, killing his family and leaving him disfigured, forcing him to wear the armor and mask.
As revenge, Doom kills Steve’s son in front of him.
Doom announces that the Avengers are coming, and Latveria prepares for war. The Fantastic Four, the Avengers, and the X-Men unite and march on Latveria. Thor prays to Odin, who sends an army from Valhalla to join the battle.
A massive war erupts as the Earths begin to collide. Eventually, the universes crash into each other and are destroyed - killing everyone.
Everyone except Doom.
It’s revealed that he stole Loki’s powers.

That truth has practical force in the believer’s life. First John 1:9 does not say to explain our sins but to “confess our sins.” Confession means agreeing with God about what occurred. There is no cleansing power in carefully arranging blame until everybody but the sinner appears responsible. The world offers endless vocabulary for avoiding moral ownership, but Scripture keeps using unpleasantly simple words: sin, lust, pride, bitterness, lying, fornication, wrath, covetousness, unbelief. The Bible does not need a public relations department. God is not trying to improve sin’s image. Once a believer stops defending the pattern, he can deal honestly with the individual acts. A guarded mind remembers that recurring excuses may be the wallpaper covering recurring rebellion.

6. Moses Fell Before God Because Israel Had Nothing to Plead

Verse 25 returns to Moses’ intercession: “Thus I fell down before the LORD forty days and forty nights, as I fell down at the first; because the LORD had said he would destroy you.” Moses does not spend those forty days presenting a balanced assessment of Israel’s positive qualities. He does not tell God that the nation had tremendous potential, many sincere people, or a difficult childhood in Egypt. He understands that when guilt has been established, mercy cannot be demanded as wages. He therefore pleads, “O Lord GOD, destroy not thy people and thine inheritance” (Deuteronomy 9:26). Notice the possessive pronouns: thy people, thine inheritance. Moses’ appeal begins not with what Israel deserves but with whom Israel belongs to. Their hope rests outside themselves.

Then Moses appeals to redemption: “which thou hast redeemed through thy greatness, which thou hast brought forth out of Egypt with a mighty hand” (Deuteronomy 9:26). Israel had not redeemed itself. It had not organized a slave revolt, defeated Pharaoh’s army, or engineered the Red Sea crossing. Redemption was God’s work. Moses places God’s own mighty acts before Him in prayer. The same nation now guilty of rebellion was the nation God had publicly claimed and brought out of Egypt. That does not make their sin insignificant; it makes their preservation a matter of God’s covenant purpose. Moses is not arguing, “They are good.” He is arguing, “They are thine.” There is a profound difference. Human merit makes a poor foundation for intercession because the first honest inspection usually discovers cracks everywhere.

For the Church Age believer, salvation rests even more plainly outside human merit. “Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us” (Titus 3:5). That verse does not turn Deuteronomy into Church doctrine; it confirms the broader biblical principle that fallen man cannot build his standing before God upon his own righteousness. The Christian’s security is grounded in Christ’s finished work, not an ability to maintain a flawless wilderness record. Romans 5:9 says believers are “justified by his blood.” The safest ground before God is never the catalogue of our accomplishments. It is what God Himself has provided. Religious pride brings a résumé. Faith points to the Redeemer.
